challenges.headline: Fixed lead time, one recipient
challenges.premise: The request implies a single notification with an implicit lead time and an implicit 'the client' as recipient.
challenges.alternative: This platform already models Contacts by role (billing/HR/operational) and rules that vary by client/contract — lead time and recipient are almost never uniform across clients in practice.
challenges.consequence: Hardcoding a lead time and a flat recipient means the first client who wants 30 days instead of 15, or wants the operational contact instead of HR, forces a rebuild of the trigger rather than a config change.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether lead time and recipient roles need to be configurable per client/contract before writing the trigger logic.

challenges.headline: One-time alert assumption
challenges.premise: The request reads as 'send a notification' — a single fire-and-forget action.
challenges.alternative: Missions get extended, ended early or cancelled after the alert is scheduled; a real build needs to recalculate, cancel or resend, not just fire once.
challenges.consequence: Without a defined recalculation policy, mission changes will produce duplicate alerts (annoying) or missed ones (the exact failure this feature exists to prevent), undermining the feature's own purpose.
challenges.recommendation: Design the trigger as a recalculated schedule tied to the mission's current end date, with explicit rules for extension/cancellation, before building the notification itself.

challenges.headline: Scoped as notification-only
challenges.premise: The request frames this purely as an alert to people.
challenges.alternative: End-of-mission is already a named platform event other automation (final invoicing, offboarding, access revocation) will eventually want to hook into.
challenges.consequence: Building a narrow, single-purpose notification now risks a second, separate implementation later when invoicing or offboarding automation needs the same trigger, duplicating the date-scanning logic.
challenges.recommendation: Scope this as a generic 'mission approaching end' event with the notification as its first subscriber, even if only the notification ships now.

Generalize the date-based lead-time scheduler so it can later serve other expiry-driven alerts (e.g. contract end, document retention) instead of being mission-specific.

challenges.premise: The request treats the notification recipients as a known, stable set.

challenges.headline: Fixed-offset alert ignores date drift
challenges.premise: The notification is assumed to fire once, at a fixed window before the recorded end date.
challenges.alternative: Mission end dates routinely move — extension, early termination, cancellation. A single alert computed once against a snapshot date will misfire or go silent when the date changes.
challenges.consequence: Without explicit handling, a changed end date either produces a stale alert already sent for the wrong date, or no alert at all if recalculation isn't triggered.
challenges.recommendation: Define the trigger as reactive to date changes (recompute on every Mission update), not a one-time schedule computed at creation.

challenges.alternative: A pure notification (inform a human, they act) and an automation trigger (system creates an invoice/task automatically) are different builds with different failure modes, idempotency needs and sync/async concerns.
challenges.consequence: Scoping this as 'notification + maybe automation' risks silently growing into a multi-system trigger chain that wasn't estimated or reviewed for idempotency and rollback.
challenges.recommendation: Decide now whether this ships as notification-only in v1, with automation explicitly deferred and separately scoped.

challenges.consequence: Wrong or incomplete recipients silently defeats the entire feature — the same failure mode the feature is meant to fix.
challenges.recommendation: Map out the recipient matrix (by role, by client, by mission type) with the client before building the routing logic.
